justification: The article delivers on its stated angle. The O(n) heapify claim is made empirically as well as visually: Figure 3 walks the exact per-level accounting (1 node at h=3, 2 at h=2, 4 at h=1, 8 leaves doing zero work, summing to 11 vs. a naive 15x3=45 bound), the prose then generalizes that to the closed-form sum-of-h/2^(h+1) argument, and the id=heapify-cost block measures comparisons-per-element for bottom-up build vs. one-at-a-time insert across n=1000..8000, showing build/n flat at ~1.85 and insert/n drifting from 2.14 to 2.24 — a real, hand-checkable empirical signature of O(n) vs. an insert path carrying a log factor, not an assertion. This is a genuine differentiator: Wikipedia's Binary_heap page (fetched this round) derives the same O(n) bound mathematically but in pseudocode with no measurement; GeeksforGeeks's heap-data-structure page (fetched this round) is a thin index page with no heapify proof at all; Microsoft's own PriorityQueue reference docs (fetched this round, remarks section read in full) state facts but derive nothing. The BCL-caveats angle is equally well executed and independently verified: I re-fetched all four .NET/runtime sources cited (PriorityQueue Class remarks, Remove Method remarks, Dequeue Method exceptions section, and PriorityQueue.cs on GitHub) and every quoted or paraphrased claim is verbatim-accurate — 'Implements an array-backed, quaternary min-heap' and 'the type does not guarantee first-in-first-out semantics for elements of equal priority' from the class remarks, 'private const int Arity = 4' and the Heapify()-on-construction behavior from the source, 'the method performs a linear-time scan of every element in the heap, removing the first value found to match the element parameter' plus the non-deterministic-duplicate-removal remark from Remove's docs, and the InvalidOperationException-on-empty-queue fact from Dequeue's Exceptions section. The Sedgewick & Wayne quote ('Sink-based heap construction is linear time') was independently fetched and matches verbatim; the CLRS chapter-6 citation is used correctly under the brief's rule for unopenable textbooks (chapter only, no invented page number). All 6 front-matter sources resolve to at least one inline citation in the body — no orphaned sources. Cross-link handling is correct and is the article's strongest structural decision: the 'A generation counter' section explicitly names what dijkstra-shortest-path.md already covers (lazy deletion via a visited set, cheap because a vertex's distance improves at most once), states why that trick doesn't generalize, and then builds a materially different mechanism (a per-key generation/version counter for priorities that can change repeatedly, e.g. a job scheduler) rather than re-deriving Dijkstra's relax-and-skip-stale-entries walkthrough. I grepped dijkstra-shortest-path.md and confirmed its lazy-deletion trace tables and 'stale' output are not reproduced here. No filler: the opening paragraph states a concrete comparative fact (unsorted array O(1) insert/O(n) min vs. sorted array's mirror image) and immediately names what the article will do; there is no restated-title sentence, no 'in this article,' no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways heading, and the piece ends on a decrease-key exercise rather than a summary paragraph. No placeholder, lorem ipsum, or NEEDS_MARKUS markers found (grepped). No ad code of any kind (grepped for adsbygoogle/googleads/ins class ad, zero hits). Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: the title ('Binary Heaps: Sift, Heapify, and PriorityQueue in C#') and description both name exactly what the body delivers, with no superlatives or unearned claims.
